claims.text: Surface segregation of lower-melting components governs the onset of premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles.
Surface segregation forms a compositionally distinct surface layer.
A surface layer enriched in lower-melting components has a lower local melting point than a uniformly mixed nanoparticle.
Rapid quenching can produce HEA nanoparticles with a homogeneous elemental distribution and minimal initial surface segregation.
Annealing at 0.5–0.7 times the solidus temperature promotes surface diffusion and segregation of lower-melting elements.
Thermally activated diffusion transports lower-melting elements to the nanoparticle surface.
The resulting surface composition gradient causes premelting to initiate at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-initiated premelting modifies the overall melting behavior of the nanoparticle.
Segregation-inducing annealing will lower the premelting onset temperature relative to homogeneous quenched nanoparticles.
Segregation-inducing annealing will broaden the melting transition relative to homogeneous quenched nanoparticles.
Homogeneously quenched HEA nanoparticles have a higher and sharper premelting or melting onset than segregated nanoparticles.
The predicted segregation effect should be observable across nanoparticle sizes from 2 to 50 nm.
The predicted effect applies to HEA systems containing a significant fraction of relatively fusible elements.
Surface effects dominate the relevant behavior in HEA nanoparticles below approximately 50 nm.
Larger or bulk samples may have their melting behavior governed by mechanisms other than surface segregation.
Particle size, alloy composition, and annealing duration affect the magnitude of the premelting-temperature reduction.
Grain-boundary diffusion may contribute secondarily to the observed melting behavior.
